cord serum levels of thyrotrophin (TSH) and thyroglobulin were related to the development of the respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants.

Tg cord serum values in preterm infants increase with gestation age, and that Tg and TSh cord serum values are significantly higher in infants who developed respiratory distress syndrome (compared to infants who did not).

cord serum thyroglobulin levels are higher in preterm infants with respiratory distress syndrome (compared to those without respiratory distress syndrome) and that cord serum Tg levels increase with increasing gestation age.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Tg levels in cord serum of RDS infants are high because of the immaturity of the thyroid gland and that the TSH levels are high because of a feedback mechanism of the thyroid gland to the pituitary gland.

the cord serum levels of Tg and Tg in RDS infants are related to birth weight, and not to the severity of the RDS, but that the cord serum TSH levels in RDS and non-RDS infants are not related to birth weight.
Tg and Tg cord serum level is a good indicator for the maturity of the thyroid gland.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the high Tg serum levels in preterm infants, especially in RDS infants, are not related to the TSH levels.
Tg and TSh cord blood levels are not influenced by perinatal factors, but that Tg cord blood levels are increased in RDS infants.
the high Tg cord serum values found in RDS infants are not due to the presence of RDS, but to the immaturity of the thyroid and liver.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Tg cord serum level may be an early predictor of RDS.
Tg and Tg/TSH ratios are useful in predicting the development of respiratory distress syndrome.
the thyroid gland of preterm infants is not fully functional at the time of birth and that the Tg and TSh cord serum levels in preterm infants are influenced by the RDS.
